# What Is Midjourney's Relax Mode? A Plain-English Guide

You're halfway through a creative idea, you've tried six different prompts (the text instructions you type to tell the AI what to draw), and Midjourney tells you you're out of fast GPU time for the month. The creative spark is right there — but the tool wants you to wait, or pay more. That's exactly the kind of moment **Relax mode** is built for.

## What Relax mode actually does

Midjourney (an AI image generation tool — think of it as a digital artist you talk to using text) gives you two main speeds: **Fast mode** and **Relax mode**. Fast mode pushes your image to the front of the queue and returns it in seconds, drawing on your monthly **fast GPU time** (the chunk of computing power your subscription includes). Relax mode lets the AI work on your image in the background, on spare server capacity. It takes longer — sometimes several minutes — but it doesn't eat into your fast GPU time.

The trade-off is simple: speed for sustainability. If you're not in a rush, Relax is a great way to keep creating when your fast minutes run low.

## How to switch it on

The cleanest way to switch modes inside Midjourney's Discord app is with two simple **slash commands** (short instructions you type that start with a `/`):

- Type **`/relax`** and press Enter to switch to Relax mode.
- Type **`/fast`** and press Enter to switch back to Fast mode.

Midjourney replies in chat to confirm which mode you're now in. If you use Midjourney's web app at midjourney.com, the mode toggle lives in the generation interface — the exact placement has shifted over time, so the easiest move is to look near the Generate button or check Midjourney's official help docs for the current layout.

A quick note on access: Relax mode has historically been available on **Standard plans and above**, though pricing and tiers can change. It's worth checking Midjourney's current pricing page for the latest details before you plan a big project around it.

## When Relax mode shines

Relax mode is built for moments when speed doesn't matter but the creative work still needs to happen. A few good fits:

- **Exploring variations** of an image you already like — queue up many versions and let them arrive gradually.
- **Personal or study projects** where there's no deadline pressing.
- **Late-night idea sessions** when your fast minutes are spent but the inspiration is flowing.
- **Refining a final image** where the composition is right and you just want the AI to polish details.

There is a soft cap on Relax usage during peak hours, so don't expect unlimited instant throughput — but for unhurried work, it's generous.

## Three prompts to try in Relax mode

If you want to test the difference, here are three example prompts you can paste straight in:

1. *"a quiet kitchen at sunrise, soft window light, watercolour illustration"*
2. *"a vintage travel poster for a coastal town, muted colours, art deco style"*
3. *"a fox curled up reading a book in a cosy library, warm lamp light, storybook style"*

Run the same prompt in both modes and compare — sometimes a slower journey gets you somewhere better.

## What this means for you

- **If you're creating for fun or study**: Relax mode is your friend once your fast minutes run out. Treat it like sending a piece of writing to a friend for feedback — slower, but still useful, and you can keep experimenting without watching the meter.
- **If you create content for work**: Use Fast mode for client-facing deadlines, then switch to Relax for your own R&D (research and development — basically your experimentation time). It keeps billable hours cleanly separate from creative play.
- **If you're brand new to AI image tools**: Don't worry about modes on day one. Start with whatever's on by default, get comfortable writing prompts, and come back to Relax once you've used up a few fast generations.

## Wrap-up

Relax mode is a small feature with a useful idea behind it: creative work doesn't always need to be instant. Switch to it when speed doesn't matter, save your fast minutes for when it does, and you'll get more value out of your subscription without changing how you prompt.

**Try this today:** open Midjourney, type `/relax`, and re-run a prompt you used last week. Compare the new result to the original.
